passage: I run the tea stall opposite the factory gate, so I saw the whole thing. For a month, Sudha and her college group had stood there every Saturday with placards about the black water in the canal. Some of the older protesters shouted 'Murderers!' at the workers going in. Sudha didn't. She said good morning to them, the same people every week. This Saturday the manager, Jagdish-ji, came out angry and said their pamphlet had the wrong numbers. Sudha asked to see his figures. She read them, standing right there, and said, 'You're right about this one. We'll correct it. But the canal is still black.' Jagdish-ji looked surprised. He accepted a cup of tea from me and stayed talking with her for half an hour. The next week, the new pamphlets had the corrected number. I don't know what will happen to the canal.

qa.q: What did some of the older protesters shout at the workers?
qa.a: 'Murderers!'

qa.q: How might Jagdish-ji have felt when Sudha admitted the mistake?
qa.a: Surprised and a little disarmed, since he came out angry and was met with honesty.

qa.q: What in Sudha's approach keeps the movement credible?
qa.a: She stays firm about the canal but checks the manager's figures, corrects the pamphlet and greets the workers as people.

qa.q: How might the workers going in see Sudha compared with the shouting protesters?
qa.a: They probably find Sudha easier to respect, since she greets them every week instead of calling them murderers.

grounding: A tea-stall owner's account of a young protester who stays firm on the cause while checking facts and treating opponents as people.

passage: Monday: Sunaina's campaign group for the street vendors of Park Road met in a café. Mahima showed a forwarded message: the ward officer had supposedly taken bribes from a mall developer. 'Let's post it tonight,' someone said. Sunaina hesitated. 'Do we have proof?' No one did. The group grumbled that she was being soft. Thursday: Sunaina called two vendors and a local journalist. The bribe story traced back to an anonymous account with no evidence. She told the group; Mahima admitted she'd been ready to post it. The following Monday: the group met the ward officer, Mr Deshmukh. Sunaina presented the vendors' real losses and a plan for fixed spots, and thanked him for his time. He didn't agree to everything, but he agreed to a second meeting.

qa.q: What did the forwarded message claim about the ward officer?
qa.a: That he had taken bribes from a mall developer.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when the group called her soft?
qa.a: Sunaina felt uncomfortable and a bit alone, but steady in wanting proof before posting.

qa.q: Why did checking the bribe story protect the campaign?
qa.a: Posting an unproven claim would have cost the movement credibility; the checked facts let them meet Mr Deshmukh with real numbers.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel after learning the story was unproven?
qa.a: Embarrassed and relieved, having been ready to post it.

grounding: Over a week a young campaigner holds firm on the cause while insisting on facts and treating an official respectfully.

passage: Mohit, you're angry at the people who oppose your campaign? Let your Kalyani ajji tell you about 1986. The women of our village wanted the liquor shop near the school closed; men were drinking away their wages. We sat outside it every Sunday. Some women wanted to burn the shop down. I said no. The owner, Shankarappa, had children in the same school. So we sat outside singing, and I took him water when it was hot. Once our leaflet said he'd sold to children. He showed me his register; he hadn't. We printed a correction. People laughed at us for that. But when the district officer came, Shankarappa himself told him the women had been honest. The shop moved to the highway that year. Stay firm, Mohit. Just stay human.

qa.q: Where did the liquor shop move?
qa.a: To the highway.

qa.q: How might Shankarappa have felt when Kalyani brought him water in the heat?
qa.a: Surprised and perhaps touched, treated as a person even by those protesting his shop.

qa.q: Which choice in the story gave the women credibility?
qa.a: Checking Shankarappa's register and printing a correction when the leaflet was wrong, which led him to vouch for their honesty.

qa.q: How might the women who wanted to burn the shop have felt about Kalyani's stand?
qa.a: Frustrated at first, perhaps, but the peaceful, honest approach won in the end.

grounding: A grandmother recalls a village campaign that stayed firm while checking facts and treating the opponent as human.

passage: Charu, you asked why I missed your birthday. Honestly, this is Ayesha hitting a wall. For eight months I've been at the animal shelter every evening after work and all weekend. Feeding, cleaning, rescue calls at midnight. I stopped going to the gym, I snapped at Ammi, and my manager warned me about mistakes at work. Every time I thought of taking a day off, I felt like a monster, because who'd feed the puppies? Last week I fell asleep on the shelter floor, and a new volunteer, Divya, found me there at six in the morning. She said, 'You can't carry this alone.' The coordinator made a rota after that. I'm on three evenings now, not seven. I still feel guilty. But I'm sleeping.

qa.q: How many evenings is Ayesha on the rota now?
qa.a: Three evenings, not seven.

qa.q: What did Ayesha feel when thinking of taking a day off?
qa.a: Guilty, 'like a monster', worried about who would feed the puppies.

qa.q: What change made Ayesha's service more sustainable?
qa.a: The coordinator's rota, which shared the load so Ayesha now does three evenings instead of every day.

qa.q: How might Divya have felt finding Ayesha on the shelter floor at six in the morning?
qa.a: Worried and concerned, which is why Divya spoke up that Ayesha couldn't carry it alone.

grounding: A committed volunteer gives so much that health, work and family suffer, feels guilty about slowing down, and is helped by a shared rota.

passage: March: Vinita taught at the free evening tuition centre in the basti near her office four nights a week, and loved it. The children called her 'Vinita didi' and waited at the door. June: she was there six nights, plus Sunday planning. She had headaches every day. She missed her cousin's engagement, and her team leader asked if everything was okay. When she thought about cutting down, she pictured little Raju waiting at the door and felt sick with guilt. August: Kavitha, the centre coordinator, sat her down. 'You've been carrying the whole Class 6 batch. That's my mistake as much as yours.' Kavitha found two more volunteers and made a rota. Vinita now teaches two nights. On her first free Wednesday, she slept eleven hours.

qa.q: How many nights does Vinita teach now?
qa.a: Two nights.

qa.q: What did Vinita feel when she thought about cutting down?
qa.a: Sick with guilt, picturing little Raju waiting at the door.

qa.q: How did Kavitha help make Vinita's service sustainable?
qa.a: She admitted the load was unfair, found two more volunteers and made a rota.

qa.q: How might Vinita's team leader have seen her in June?
qa.a: Probably concerned, noticing something was wrong at work, which is why the team leader asked if everything was okay.

grounding: Over months a volunteer takes on so much that work and health suffer, feels guilty about easing off, and is helped by shared load.

passage: Vaibhav, you've been at the food bank every night for two months. Sit, and let your Yamini aunty tell you about 2005. After the floods that year, I worked with a relief group in Mumbai. I thought if I rested, someone would go hungry. I skipped meals, lied to my mother about sleeping, worked sixteen-hour days. One morning I fainted in the warehouse, and a volunteer doctor checked me and sent me home. I cried, not from pain but from guilt. Then our group leader, Farooq bhai, made a rule: no one works more than four days a week. Some people were angry. But the relief work lasted two years instead of two months, because people didn't break. Rest isn't betrayal, beta. It's how the work survives.

qa.q: What rule did Farooq bhai make?
qa.a: No one works more than four days a week.

qa.q: Why did young Yamini cry after being sent home?
qa.a: From guilt, feeling that resting meant letting people down.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the relief work sustainable?
qa.a: Farooq bhai's rule limiting everyone to four days a week, which kept volunteers from breaking and let the work last two years.

qa.q: How might the other volunteers have felt about the four-day rule?
qa.a: Some were angry at first, but it likely saved them from burning out too.

grounding: An aunt recalls burning out as a relief volunteer and how limits and a shared load let the work last.

passage:
Hi Abhinav,
I've been thinking about Sunday's meeting. You said the clean-river campaign only moves because of the rallies, and that the 'office people' don't count. I got angry and said nothing, so here goes.
I've watched this group for a year. Meher does the accounts every night so our donations stay clean. Sanjay drives the old van to every site. Pritam dadi has written seventy letters to the council by hand. Laila designs the posters you hold up. None of them ever speaks on the mic.
You're a great speaker. The rallies matter. But when you say only speeches count, the quiet ones feel invisible, and some have stopped coming.
Can we thank them properly at the next meeting? Together?
Amandeep

qa.q: How many letters has Pritam dadi written to the council?
qa.a: Seventy letters, by hand.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when Abhinav dismissed the 'office people'?
qa.a: Amandeep felt angry but stayed silent at the meeting, then felt the need to speak up in writing.

qa.q: What does Amandeep suggest, and why would it help?
qa.a: Thanking the quiet contributors together at the next meeting, so they feel valued and the group's resentment eases.

qa.q: How might Meher feel hearing that only speeches count?
qa.a: Invisible and unappreciated, despite doing the accounts every night.

grounding: An observer of a campaign sees that quiet organisers, drivers, letter-writers and designers matter as much as speakers.

passage: Yogesh, thanks for asking about the tenants' campaign. I'm Ritu, and for a long time I thought the only people who mattered were the ones on stage. Our leader, Salma-ji, gives speeches that make grown men cry. But after two years of watching, I saw how many others it takes. Bose uncle, who never speaks, knows every tenant's name and phones each one before every meeting. Neelu types up the documents at night after her shift. A retired teacher sends us a small donation every month and has never come to a single rally. When some volunteers complained that Salma-ji got all the credit, I stood up and listed the others by name. The room went quiet, then clapped. Nobody's too small in a movement.

qa.q: What does Bose uncle do before every meeting?
qa.a: Phones each tenant.

qa.q: What did Ritu come to feel about the quiet workers over two years?
qa.a: Ritu came to feel appreciation and respect for the quiet workers, after first thinking only the people on stage mattered.

qa.q: How did Ritu reduce resentment when volunteers complained?
qa.a: By standing up and naming the quieter contributors, so everyone's work was recognised.

qa.q: How might Neelu feel being named at the meeting?
qa.a: Seen and appreciated for typing documents at night after her shift, work that usually goes unnoticed.

grounding: An observer comes to see that a movement needs quiet organisers, typists and donors, and naming them eases resentment.

passage: I've volunteered with the river-bank clean-up group in Guwahati for three years, and I've watched Pranav and Bhupen closely. Pranav is the one on the news, leading chants, giving interviews in his bright orange cap. Bhupen is the one nobody photographs. He arrives at five to count the sacks, fixes the broken boat engine and keeps the volunteer list on his phone. Last month a few people muttered that Pranav 'takes all the glory'. Pranav overheard. At the next gathering, he handed Bhupen the megaphone and said, 'Without him, there are no sacks, no boat, no us.' Bhupen went red and said only, 'Thank you. Now, the sacks.' People laughed. I can't know what Bhupen feels inside. But he came earlier than ever the next week.

qa.q: What does Bhupen fix?
qa.a: The broken boat engine.

qa.q: What does the narrator seem to feel watching Pranav hand Bhupen the megaphone?
qa.a: The narrator seems moved and hopeful, noting that Bhupen came earlier than ever afterwards, while admitting they can't know Bhupen's inner feelings.

qa.q: What did Pranav do to reduce the resentment in the group?
qa.a: He publicly credited Bhupen, handing him the megaphone and saying the group couldn't work without him.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt being handed the megaphone?
qa.a: Embarrassed but valued, going red and then turning it into a joke about the sacks.

grounding: A volunteer's account of a group where the visible speaker publicly credits a quiet worker, easing resentment.

passage: Jahnavi, you asked what the flood camp was really like. I'm Neelam, and I'm still tired, three weeks later. I went with the district relief team to a school turned into a shelter near Silchar. Four hundred people, one kitchen. I peeled potatoes till my fingers went white, sorted donated clothes, held babies so their mothers could sleep. One night I wanted to take a boat to a village I'd heard was cut off. The team lead said no: 'We don't send untrained people into currents. The rescue unit goes.' I was furious. The next morning the rescue unit brought eleven people back safely. I cried in the kitchen, from tiredness and relief. I felt useful and completely overwhelmed, both at once.

qa.q: How many people were in the shelter?
qa.a: Four hundred.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when the team lead refused the boat trip?
qa.a: Furious and frustrated, wanting to help the cut-off village directly.

qa.q: Why was the team lead's 'no' the right call?
qa.a: Untrained people in strong currents could become victims themselves; the trained rescue unit brought eleven people back safely.

qa.q: What might the mothers have felt when Neelam held their babies?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful to finally sleep in a crowded shelter.

grounding: A young volunteer in flood relief feels tired, useful and overwhelmed, and learns that working within the organised effort keeps help safe.

passage: Day one: when fever cases spread through the colony, Naveen signed up with the ward health team. His job was to go door to door with Pradeep, the health worker, checking for standing water and handing out leaflets. By evening he had visited sixty homes and felt useful and proud. Day three: an old man in Block D begged Naveen to take his feverish wife to hospital on his scooter. Naveen almost did, then remembered the team's rule: call the helpline and the team doctor. The ambulance came in twenty minutes. Naveen went home and sat in the dark, shaking, overwhelmed by how much was wrong. Day six: the team met. Pradeep showed a map: breeding spots down by half. 'Your street did that,' he told Naveen. Naveen slept properly for the first time that week.

qa.q: How many homes had Naveen visited by the end of day one?
qa.a: Sixty homes.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel sitting in the dark on day three?
qa.a: Shaken and overwhelmed by how much was wrong, after the scare with the feverish woman.

qa.q: What choice on day three kept the help safe and effective?
qa.a: Calling the helpline and the team doctor instead of taking the woman on his scooter, so the ambulance came in twenty minutes.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Naveen's work by day six?
qa.a: As genuinely valuable, pointing to the map and crediting Naveen's street for cutting the breeding spots.

grounding: Over a week a young volunteer in a health drive feels useful, then overwhelmed, and relies on the organised team's rules.

passage: Kalyani, you're leaving for the relief camp tomorrow? Let your Karthik mama tell you something from the big cyclone, when I was your age. I went to Nagapattinam with a college group, full of fire. On the first day I tried to do everything: carry sacks, cook, pull things out of damaged houses. By night I'd cut my hand on a tin sheet and was useless. The camp leader, a retired army nurse we called Mary aunty, sat me down. 'One job, done well, inside the team. That's how we save people.' She put me on the water-distribution line. Twelve days, same job, clean water for two thousand people. I was tired, and sometimes overwhelmed. But I was useful, and I was safe. Choose one job, and do it with the team.

qa.q: What job did Mary aunty give young Karthik?
qa.a: The water-distribution line.

qa.q: How did young Karthik feel at the end of the first day?
qa.a: Exhausted and frustrated, having hurt his hand trying to do everything.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made young Karthik's help effective and safe?
qa.a: Accepting one job inside the team, on the water line, instead of trying to do everything alone.

qa.q: What might Mary aunty have seen in young Karthik that first night?
qa.a: An eager but overstretched volunteer who would burn out or get hurt without a clear role.

grounding: An uncle recalls cyclone relief work, tiring and overwhelming, made useful and safe by one role inside an organised team.

subtype: Staying safe and lawful in action [Response]
passage: Emil and Tariq spent two weeks planning the students' march for cheaper public transport in Copenhagen. They registered the route with the police, trained twenty stewards in bright vests, and printed a card for every marcher: stay on the route, no masks, and if anything turns violent, walk away. On the day, three thousand people walked peacefully, drumming and singing. Near the square, a small group in black hoods started throwing bottles at a shop window. Tariq's stomach dropped. Emil grabbed the megaphone. 'This march is over. Everyone, follow the stewards to the park!' Some marchers booed; they wanted to stay. But most followed. The next day the papers wrote about the bottle-throwers, and also that the organisers had called the march off at once.

qa.q: How many stewards did Emil and Tariq train?
qa.a: Twenty stewards.

qa.q: What did Tariq feel when the bottles started flying?
qa.a: Tariq's stomach dropped, alarmed and afraid that the peaceful march would be ruined or someone hurt.

qa.q: What safety planning helped Emil and Tariq act quickly?
qa.a: Registering the route, training stewards and giving every marcher a card saying to walk away if things turned violent.

qa.q: How might the marchers who booed feel about ending early?
qa.a: Disappointed and frustrated, wanting to stay, though leaving kept them away from the violence.

grounding: Organisers plan a march for safety and peace, and end it at once when a small group turns violent.

subtype: Staying safe and lawful in action [Response]
passage: In the student union office, Kiran pinned up the plan for Friday's sit-in against the library's shorter hours: two hours, outside the library, no blocking doors, first-aid kit by the pillar. Afreen, the union secretary, wanted more. 'Let's lock the library gates. They'll have to listen.' Kiran shook her head. 'That blocks other students and could get people suspended. We sit, we speak, we leave.' Kiran had also asked the university's legal-aid cell about students' right to gather on campus, and printed their helpline on every flyer. On Friday, two hundred students sat reading library books aloud. When a group from another hostel arrived shouting and kicking the gate, Kiran stood up and ended the sit-in. The next week, the dean agreed to a meeting.

qa.q: How long was the sit-in planned to last?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt when Kiran refused to lock the gates?
qa.a: Frustrated and impatient, wanting stronger pressure to force the administration to listen.

qa.q: What did Kiran do to keep the action safe and lawful?
qa.a: Kept it peaceful and time-limited, avoided blocking doors, checked students' rights with the legal-aid cell and ended the sit-in when others turned aggressive.

qa.q: How might the other students using the library see a peaceful sit-in?
qa.a: They can still get in and study, so they are more likely to sympathise with the cause.

grounding: A student organiser plans a peaceful, lawful sit-in, refuses tactics that harm others, and ends it when things turn aggressive.

subtype: Staying safe and lawful in action [Response]
passage:
Subject: Plan for Saturday's vendors' rally
Hi Sumit,
Before Saturday, a few things I want us both clear on.
1. We march only on the route the police approved: from the old market to the municipal office.
2. Each block of twenty vendors has one volunteer with a whistle and a list of phone numbers, including the free legal-aid line.
3. No sticks, no burning anything. If anyone brings them, we ask them to leave.
4. If the crowd turns violent, we stop and walk everyone back. I know some of the younger vendors will call us cowards. I'd rather be called a coward than see Hanif chacha's cart burned or anyone hurt.
Our cause is fair. It stays fair only if our way is too.
Call me tonight?
Imran

qa.q: Where does the approved route go?
qa.a: From the old market to the municipal office.

qa.q: What is Imran worried about?
qa.a: Imran is anxious that the crowd could turn violent and someone could be hurt, or a cart like Hanif chacha's burned.

qa.q: Which parts of the plan protect people's safety and rights?
qa.a: The approved route, block volunteers with whistles and the legal-aid number, no sticks or burning, and walking everyone back if violence starts.

qa.q: How might the younger vendors see the rule to stop if things turn violent?
qa.a: Some may see it as cowardly, wanting to push harder, even though it protects them.

grounding: An organiser's plan for a vendors' rally that puts safety, rights and peaceful methods first, and walks away from violence.

subtype: Pressure to protect the institution's name [Receiver]
passage: Kashish, can I tell you what happened with the dean? It's Hrithik, and I'm a mess. I saw a group of final-years with the leaked chemistry paper the night before the exam. I reported it, in writing. Today the dean called me in. He didn't shout. He just said, very kindly, that a leak story would 'damage our college's name', that my batch's placements might suffer, and did I really want to be responsible for that? He slid a withdrawal form across the table. I felt so guilty, as if I was the one who'd done something wrong. I almost signed. I didn't. I went straight to Professor Nair, who chairs the exam committee, and she said the committee has to look into it and that my name stays confidential. But I keep thinking about that form.

qa.q: What did the dean slide across the table?
qa.a: A withdrawal form.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel in the dean's office?
qa.a: Guilty and afraid, as if Hrithik were the wrongdoer, and close to signing the form.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do instead of signing, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Went straight to Professor Nair, who chairs the exam committee and confirmed the complaint must be examined and kept confidential.

qa.q: How might Professor Nair view the dean's pressure?
qa.a: She seems to see the complaint as something to be examined properly, not buried for the college's name.

grounding: A student who reports cheating is pressured to withdraw for the college's reputation and feels guilt and fear, but finds a proper channel.

subtype: Pressure to protect the institution's name [Receiver]
passage: Monday: Sharmila submitted a written complaint to the college's internal committee: a guest lecturer had been sending her late-night messages and touching her shoulder in the lab. Her friend Manoj went with her to the office. Wednesday: the head of department called her in. 'This lecturer brings us a big research grant. Think about the college's name. Think about your own.' Sharmila left shaking and told Manoj she would withdraw. She felt guilty, as if she had started a fire. That evening Manoj went with her to Dr Ansari, the committee's chairperson. Dr Ansari listened, told Sharmila it was not her fault and that no one could pressure her to withdraw, and that same night wrote to the principal about the head's interference. The next Monday: the lecturer was suspended pending an inquiry. Sharmila still felt watched in the corridors. But she did not withdraw.

qa.q: What did the head of department say about the lecturer?
qa.a: That he brings the college a big research grant.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel after meeting the head of department?
qa.a: Shaken and guilty, as if she had started a fire, and ready to withdraw the complaint.

qa.q: What made the difference after the head's pressure?
qa.a: Manoj going with her to Dr Ansari, who listened, said it wasn't her fault, stopped the pressure and wrote to the principal that same night.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt watching Sharmila decide to withdraw?
qa.a: Worried and protective, which is why he went with her to Dr Ansari that evening.

grounding: A student who reports harassment is pressured to withdraw for the college's name, feels guilt and fear, and is protected by the committee chair the same day.

subtype: Pressure to protect the institution's name [Receiver]
passage: Lalremsiami, you asked if it's worth reporting. Let your Gurpreet aunty tell you about 1991, at my college in Chandigarh. A senior in the hostel was cornering first-year girls in the stairwell. My roommate cried every night. I went to the principal. She listened, then said, 'Beta, if this comes out, parents will stop sending their daughters here. Think of the college.' I walked out feeling like the criminal. For three days I said nothing. Then our warden, Mrs Sandhu, saw my roommate's face and asked. That same evening she called my roommate's parents and wrote to the university, and the senior was sent out of the hostel within the week. The principal never spoke to me again. I would still do it again.

qa.q: Where was the senior cornering first-year girls?
qa.a: In the hostel stairwell.

qa.q: How did young Gurpreet feel leaving the principal's office?
qa.a: Like a criminal, guilty and afraid, which kept her silent for three days.

qa.q: Which turning point in the story stopped the harassment?
qa.a: Warden Mrs Sandhu asking the roommate and, that same evening, calling her parents and writing to the university.

qa.q: What might the roommate have gone through before the warden asked?
qa.a: She cried every night, frightened and alone, while the complaint was stalled by the principal.

grounding: An aunt recalls reporting harassment and being told to protect the college's name, and the warden who acted the same day.

passage: Jomon, you told your manager about the fake overtime claims and now nobody eats with you? Sit. Your Madhuri aunty knows this feeling. In 1998, as a young nurse in Thrissur, I reported that a senior was taking medicines home from the ward store. The inquiry was quiet, and she was transferred. But the ward never forgave me. Tea-break conversations stopped when I walked in. Someone left a note in my locker: 'Snake.' My review called me 'difficult'. I nearly resigned. Then one ward aide, Thankamma chechi, started sitting next to me at lunch every single day, saying nothing special, just sitting. It was enough. One person, Jomon. Find your Thankamma. And be one for someone else.

qa.q: What was written on the note in young Madhuri's locker?
qa.a: 'Snake.'

qa.q: How did young Madhuri feel in the months after reporting?
qa.a: Isolated and hurt, close to resigning as conversations stopped when she walked in.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the isolation bearable?
qa.a: Thankamma chechi choosing to sit beside her at lunch every day, one quiet ally.

qa.q: What might Thankamma chechi have risked by sitting with Madhuri?
qa.a: Being gossiped about or isolated too, which makes her quiet support brave.

grounding: An aunt recalls being quietly ostracised after reporting wrongdoing, and how one ally made it bearable.

passage: Sunaina had reported the mess manager for pocketing money from the hostel food budget two weeks before her final exams. Now, in the small hostel of forty girls, nobody sat with her. The manager was related to half the staff, and the rumour went round that Sunaina was 'a troublemaker who wanted free food'. Someone scrawled 'chugli', telltale, on her door. With exams ten days away and the Wi-Fi 'mysteriously' off on her floor, she studied by the corridor light, eyes stinging. Then Lakshmi, from the room opposite, knocked at eleven at night with two cups of tea and her notes. 'You were right. I'm studying with you till the exams.' They sat on the floor till one. The next morning Lakshmi also wrote a supporting statement to the warden.

qa.q: What was scrawled on Sunaina's door?
qa.a: 'Chugli', meaning telltale.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel studying by the corridor light?
qa.a: Isolated and worn down, eyes stinging, shut out by the other girls with exams close.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do that mattered?
qa.a: She studied with Sunaina every night and wrote a supporting statement to the warden, standing openly beside her.

qa.q: How might the other girls see Sunaina after the rumour?
qa.a: Many seem to believe she is a troublemaker, swayed by the manager's links to the staff.

grounding: A student who reported wrongdoing is quietly isolated before exams, and one ally makes a great difference.

passage: In the coaching centre in Kota, word spread fast that Mahima was the one who'd told the director about Sir leaking test papers to his favourite batch. By Monday, the girls at her table had moved to another bench. In the group chat, someone posted a snake symbol every time she wrote. The teacher she'd reported now marked her answers harshly, and nobody said anything. Mahima started eating lunch alone in the stairwell, telling herself she didn't care. On Thursday, Aditi from the back bench sat down beside her with a lunchbox. 'I saw the leaked papers too. I should have said something. Want half my paratha?' Mahima laughed, suddenly teary. That afternoon the two of them went to the director together to report the harsh marking.

qa.q: Where did Mahima eat lunch after being frozen out?
qa.a: Alone in the stairwell.

qa.q: What did Mahima feel when Aditi sat down beside her?
qa.a: A sudden rush of relief and gratitude, laughing and teary after days of isolation.

qa.q: How did Aditi's support turn into action?
qa.a: She admitted she'd seen the leaks too, and went with Mahima to the director to report the harsh marking.

qa.q: How might the girls who moved benches see Mahima?
qa.a: As a traitor to the batch, following the group's quiet retaliation rather than thinking about the leaks.

grounding: A student who reported a teacher's wrongdoing faces quiet social retaliation, and one ally changes everything.

subtype: Told to stay quiet at work [Receiver]
passage: Rafael had been at the construction firm in Lisbon for eight months when he noticed hairline cracks in the concrete of the third-floor supports. He showed the photos to his manager, Mr Costa. Costa looked for a long time, then said, 'The client opens in three weeks. Don't make noise. It's probably cosmetic.' Rafael went home and couldn't eat. What if he was wrong? What if he lost the job his family was so proud of? At lunch the next day, his colleague Soo-ah looked at the photos. 'It's not your job to decide it's safe. It's your job to report it.' That afternoon Rafael sent the photos to the company's safety officer and copied Costa. The site was closed for inspection the next morning.

qa.q: Where did Rafael notice the cracks?
qa.a: In the concrete of the third-floor supports.

qa.q: What did Rafael feel after Costa told him not to make noise?
qa.a: Afraid for his job and doubtful of his own judgement, so upset he couldn't eat.

qa.q: What protective step did Rafael take, and why was it right?
qa.a: He sent the photos to the safety officer and copied Costa, since deciding safety isn't his call but reporting is.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah see Rafael's dilemma?
qa.a: Soo-ah sees it clearly as a safety duty, not a loyalty question, and helps Rafael see that too.

grounding: An employee who finds a safety problem is told to let it go for the company's sake, feels fear and self-doubt, and reports it properly.

subtype: Told to stay quiet at work [Receiver]
passage: On her third night shift in the private hospital's ICU, Harsha found three boxes of an injection whose expiry dates had passed. She showed Sister Ganga, the senior nurse. Sister Ganga glanced at them and slid them back onto the shelf. 'The inspection is next week. If this comes out, we lose accreditation, and all of us lose our jobs. Let it go.' Harsha nodded, then spent the rest of the shift feeling sick. Maybe the dates didn't matter? Maybe she'd misunderstood? At six in the morning, she took the boxes off the shelf, labelled them DO NOT USE, and before going home wrote to the pharmacy head and the nursing superintendent with photos. Sister Ganga didn't speak to her for a week. The pharmacy replaced the stock that day.

qa.q: How many boxes of the injection had passed their expiry dates?
qa.a: Three boxes.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel for the rest of the shift?
qa.a: Sick with worry, afraid for her job and doubting whether she had misunderstood.

qa.q: What protective steps did Harsha take?
qa.a: She took the boxes off the shelf, labelled them DO NOT USE, and wrote to the pharmacy head and nursing superintendent with photos before leaving.

qa.q: Why might Sister Ganga have told Harsha to let it go?
qa.a: She feared the hospital would lose accreditation and staff would lose jobs, and put that fear ahead of patient safety.

grounding: A young nurse told by a senior to ignore a safety problem feels fear and doubt, then takes protective steps and reports it.

subtype: Told to stay quiet at work [Receiver]
passage:
Dear Ramesh sir,
I need advice from someone outside the company. At the chemical plant, I found that our weekly waste-water readings are being 'adjusted' before they go to the pollution board. My supervisor told me, 'Everyone does it. Think of the plant, think of your career.' My team leader said the same, more kindly.
I haven't slept properly in a week. I keep wondering if I've misread the logs, if I'm the fool here. And I'm scared. My parents took a loan for my degree.
But the canal behind the plant goes to three villages.
I've saved copies of the original readings. Today I also called the company's ethics hotline and made an anonymous report, which I learned about in your class.
Can we talk this weekend?
Darshan

qa.q: Where does the canal behind the plant go?
qa.a: To three villages.

qa.q: What is Darshan feeling this week?
qa.a: Anxious and afraid for the job, and doubtful about whether the logs were misread.

qa.q: What steps has Darshan taken, and why are they sensible?
qa.a: Saving copies of the original readings and making an anonymous report to the ethics hotline, which protects the evidence and the villages while Darshan seeks outside advice.

qa.q: How might the people in the three villages be affected if the readings stay 'adjusted'?
qa.a: They could be using polluted water without knowing it.

grounding: An employee told by superiors to overlook falsified safety data feels fear and self-doubt, and reports it through a proper channel.

passage: The first time, it was only one number. Ramesh's Bengaluru sales team was short of target by two orders, and his manager, Yogesh, said, 'Book the March orders in February. Everyone does it. It keeps us all safe.' Ramesh felt a small, cold knot in his stomach, but he did it. The next month it was five orders. The knot was smaller. By June he was the one showing the new joiner how to move dates in the system. 'Relax,' he told her, hearing Yogesh's voice in his own. 'It keeps us all safe.' That night, lying awake, he realised he couldn't remember when he'd stopped feeling the knot.

qa.q: How many orders was the team short by the first time?
qa.a: Two orders.

qa.q: What happened to Ramesh's guilt over the months?
qa.a: It shrank; the cold knot got smaller each month until he couldn't remember when he'd stopped feeling it.

qa.q: What could Ramesh do now that he has noticed?
qa.a: Stop moving dates, tell the new joiner honestly that it was wrong, and raise the practice with someone above Yogesh or through the company's ethics channel.

qa.q: How might the new joiner see what Ramesh taught her?
qa.a: She may accept it as normal, since a senior told her it keeps everyone safe, and begin the same slide.

grounding: An employee joins a small fudge of numbers, and each step makes the next easier as guilt is quieted by team excuses.

passage:
'Just sign the calibration sheet,' Lokesh said, not looking up. 'We'll do the check tomorrow.'
Shalini held the pen. 'You said that last week.'
'And nothing happened, right? The machine's fine.'
'We signed it as done on the fourteenth. It wasn't.'
'Everyone signs it. The audit only looks for signatures.' He finally looked at her. 'You want the whole lab in trouble for one missed check?'
She signed. Her hand felt heavy.
The next Friday, Lokesh didn't even ask. He just left the sheet on her bench with a sticky note: 'Usual.'
Shalini stared at it. 'Usual,' she said aloud. Three weeks ago she'd never have signed. Now there was a 'usual'.
She peeled off the note and went to find the calibration kit.

qa.q: What did Lokesh's sticky note say?
qa.a: 'Usual.'

qa.q: What does Shalini's heavy hand when signing suggest?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy, knowing she was signing for a check that hadn't happened.

qa.q: What did Shalini do at the end, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She went to find the calibration kit and do the check, breaking the slide before it became normal.

qa.q: How does Lokesh seem to see the skipped checks?
qa.a: As harmless paperwork, telling himself the audit only looks for signatures and that it protects the lab.

grounding: A lab worker signs one false check under pressure, notices how quickly it became 'usual', and stops the slide.

passage: At the warehouse, our team got a bonus for every month with 'zero incidents'. The first near-miss I didn't report was small: a pallet slipped off the forklift and missed Pallavi's foot by a hand's width. Our supervisor said, 'Nobody's hurt. Don't spoil the record for the whole team.' I told myself he was right. The second time a shelf wobbled, I said nothing without even being asked. By the fourth, I was the one telling new people, 'We sort these things ourselves.' Then Pallavi fractured her wrist when that same shelf finally came down. She reported everything, including the earlier near-misses, and the shelves were all checked that week. I'm Vishal, and I still can't forgive myself for how easy each silence got.

qa.q: What was the team's bonus for?
qa.a: Every month with 'zero incidents'.

qa.q: How does Vishal feel looking back?
qa.a: Vishal feels deep guilt and regret, unable to forgive how easy each silence became.

qa.q: What could Vishal have done at the first near-miss?
qa.a: Reported it despite the supervisor's words, so the shelf could have been checked before anyone was hurt.

qa.q: What was it like for Pallavi to report everything after her injury?
qa.a: Painful and probably lonely, going against the team's record, but necessary to stop further harm.

grounding: A worker's small silence about a near-miss grows into a habit of covering up, each step easier, until someone is hurt.

passage: In the sugar-mill town near Belagavi, Tejas owed everything to his senior, Mr Hegde. Hegde had hired him, taught him the weighbridge, even come to his sister's wedding. So when Tejas noticed that farmers' cane was being under-weighed by a few kilos every load, and that Hegde signed off on it, his chest went tight. The farmers were people he saw at the chai stall. Lavanya, whose father sold cane to the mill, asked one evening, 'Appa thinks the scale is cheating him. Is it?' Tejas didn't answer. At home he wrote out the readings, then tore up the page. If he reported it, the whole office would call him a traitor, and Hegde would be ruined. If he didn't, farmers like Lavanya's father would keep losing. He sat with both, awake till dawn.

qa.q: What did Tejas notice about the farmers' cane?
qa.a: It was being under-weighed by a few kilos every load.

qa.q: Why did Tejas tear up the page of readings?
qa.a: He felt torn between loyalty and guilt, afraid of being called a traitor and of ruining Mr Hegde.

qa.q: What is one safe next step Tejas could take?
qa.a: Keep a record of the readings and talk quietly to a trusted senior or the cooperative's auditor, so the farmers are protected without Tejas acting alone.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's father feel about the weighbridge?
qa.a: Suspicious and wronged, believing the scale is cheating him, as Lavanya says.

grounding: A young engineer feels real loyalty to a senior and real duty to wronged farmers, and fear of being called a traitor.

passage: Oskar had worked in Chef Brandt's kitchen in Berlin for three years. Brandt had taken him on when no one else would and taught him everything. Tonight Oskar watched Brandt peel the date labels off a tray of chicken and stick on new ones. 'Busy weekend,' Brandt said. 'Nobody gets sick from one day.' Oskar's stomach turned. His friend Yara, at the next station, raised her eyebrows at him. Loyalty pulled one way: Brandt was like an uncle. Conscience pulled the other: a table of schoolchildren had booked for tomorrow. In the walk-in fridge, Yara whispered, 'If you don't, I will.' Oskar took a breath, moved the tray to the waste bin and quietly told Brandt he would not cook it. Brandt stared at him. 'Traitor,' he muttered.

qa.q: What did Chef Brandt do to the tray of chicken?
qa.a: Peeled off the date labels and stuck on new ones.

qa.q: What was Oskar feeling in the kitchen?
qa.a: Torn and sick, pulled by loyalty to Brandt, who was like an uncle, and by fear for the schoolchildren.

qa.q: What protective step did Oskar take?
qa.a: He moved the tray to the waste bin and quietly told Brandt he wouldn't cook it, so the food was not served.

qa.q: How might Yara see the situation?
qa.a: Yara sees the danger clearly and is ready to act, pushing Oskar with 'If you don't, I will.'

grounding: A young cook feels loyalty to a mentor and a duty to diners, fears being called a traitor, and acts to protect others.

passage: In the staff room of the Lucknow school, Irfan found the practical-exam mark sheets on Hemant sir's desk, with several low scores neatly changed to higher ones. Hemant sir had mentored him since his first day, covered his classes when his father was ill, and taught him how to handle Class 10. When Irfan asked, Hemant sir sighed. 'Our results decide next year's admissions. We protect each other here. You understand.' Irfan did understand. That was the problem. Walking home, he felt like two people: the one who loved Hemant sir, and the one who thought of the students who had actually earned their marks. Calling it out would make him a traitor in the staff room. Staying quiet would make him part of it. That night he couldn't eat.

qa.q: What had been changed on the practical-exam mark sheets?
qa.a: Several low scores had been changed to higher ones.

qa.q: What did Irfan mean by feeling like two people?
qa.a: He felt torn between loyalty and love for Hemant sir and a guilty sense of duty to students who earned their real marks.

qa.q: What could Irfan do next?
qa.a: Speak privately to Hemant sir again, and if nothing changes, take it to the principal or the board's official channel, keeping a copy of the sheets.

qa.q: How might the students who earned high marks honestly be affected?
qa.a: Their real achievement is blurred, and the results no longer tell the truth about anyone's work.

grounding: A young teacher feels loyalty to a mentor who altered marks and a duty to students, with fear of being called a traitor.
